title: {{NAME}} and the Royal Football Tournament
moral: The best teams are built on trust, not trophies.
character_anchor: Bright children's book cartoon illustration, bold outlines, vivid flat colours. {{NAME}}, a young boy with brown hair and blue eyes, wearing a royal purple soccer jersey with a small crown badge, white shorts, and purple cleats — same child, same face, same exact outfit in every image.

pages.content:
{{NAME}} was recruited to play in the Royal Invitational Tournament, which sounded impressive until he arrived and found out the other team was the Palace Guard: twelve enormous men who had all played football semi-professionally before becoming guards.

His team: himself, four kids from the village, and Princess Margaux, who had turned up in her best gown and announced she would play centre forward.

Everyone looked at everyone else.

"I'm fast," said the princess, not waiting for objections. "Let's train."

pages.content:
Princess Margaux was fast. Genuinely, embarrassingly fast.

But she had never played as part of a team before, and her natural instinct was to take the ball and solve the problem herself.

"Football isn't chess," {{NAME}} told her, after the third training session where she'd scored twice and lost the ball three times more. "You can't solve it alone."

She stopped. Looked at him. "Tell me what I'm missing."

This, {{NAME}} thought, is a person who actually wants to be good at things.

pages.content:
He taught her to look up. To see the whole pitch, not just the ball.

The tournament match was three days later. The Palace Guard played hard and fast. By half time, {{NAME}}'s team was two down.

But the Guard had not accounted for Princess Margaux's speed through the second half, or for the fact that she had spent three days learning to trust her teammates.

She set up three goals in twenty minutes, running channels, holding the ball until the last second, finding {{NAME}} exactly when he needed it.

Final score: three all.

pages.content:
The draw was enough for {{NAME}}'s team to win on goal difference.

Princess Margaux held the small tournament trophy and looked at it for a long time.

"I've won things before," she said. "Competitions where I was the best person. This is different."

"You weren't the best person this time," said {{NAME}}. "We were."

She handed him the trophy.

"You keep it," she said. "I'm keeping the feeling."

pages.content:
On the road home, {{NAME}} held the trophy in his lap and replayed the match.

The pass Margaux had made in the 72nd minute, the one that had let him score the equaliser, had been perfect. She had seen the space before he had.

In his room that night, he put the trophy on his shelf and lay looking at it.

He was almost asleep when he heard something outside: the distant thump of someone practising free kicks in the palace courtyard, long after dark.

He smiled. Some people just couldn't stop.
